notice: Hands-on labs, defined day by day. Every lab is LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT only: fictional data or isolated test systems, never production.

labs.title: Run a mini business impact analysis on a test service
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a fictional service or one you run in an isolated home or test lab. Do not interview colleagues or use production systems.
labs.goal: Practise turning business impact into MTD, RTO and RPO, and surface dependencies, before any recovery design.
prerequisites: A spreadsheet or notebook
Pick one fictional business process, for example 'agent cash-in for a mobile money service'
Cards: RTO, RPO, WRT, MTD; drill: RTO, RPO, MTD and WRT
steps: Describe the process in two sentences and name its owner.
List what it depends on: systems, data, people, suppliers, utilities, telecom links.
Estimate the impact of an outage at 1 hour, 4 hours, 1 day and 3 days: money, regulatory, reputation, safety.
Mark the point where impact becomes unacceptable: that is the MTD.
Estimate the work recovery time after a restore (checks, reconciliation) and set RTO = MTD − WRT or lower.
Set the RPO from how much data the process can lose and still be reconstructed.
Mark every single point of failure in the dependency list.
validation: RTO + WRT does not exceed MTD.
At least one external dependency is listed.
No recovery solution or vendor appears in the output: the BIA states requirements only.
rollback: Nothing to roll back: this is a paper exercise.
evidence: The completed impact table and the MTD, RTO, RPO line.
The list of single points of failure, ranked.

labs.title: Build a risk register for a fictional bank
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a new spreadsheet with fictional data only. Do not use real company risks, systems or names.
labs.goal: Turn a scenario into a working risk register with owners, ratings, treatments and an acceptance decision, and do one quantitative calculation.
prerequisites: A spreadsheet app (Excel, LibreOffice or Google Sheets)
Read the Mukuvisi Bank case study in Questions → Scenario sets
Cards: risk treatment, SLE/ARO/ALE, control types
steps: Create columns: ID, risk statement (threat + vulnerability + asset), owner, likelihood (1-5), impact (1-5), inherent score, existing controls, treatment, residual likelihood, residual impact, residual score, acceptance authority, review date.
Write five risks for the fictional Mukuvisi Bank, for example ransomware on core banking, stale policy, unclassified data, single telecom carrier, insider fraud in payments.
Score likelihood and impact for each and compute inherent score = likelihood × impact.
Choose a treatment for each (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept) and name one control per mitigated risk, labelled by type (preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating).
Re-score residual likelihood and impact after treatment and compute the residual score.
Set an appetite rule, for example residual 1-6 accepted by department head, 8-12 by executive, 15+ by board, and fill in the acceptance authority column.
For the ransomware risk, estimate asset value, exposure factor and annual rate of occurrence; compute SLE and ALE in a separate cell and compare with the annual cost of one control.
validation: Every risk names an owner from the business, not only IT.
Every risk has a treatment, a residual score and a review date.
Acceptance authority rises with residual score as your appetite rule says.
SLE = asset value × exposure factor and ALE = SLE × ARO are calculated correctly.
rollback: Nothing to roll back: the lab touches no system. Delete the spreadsheet if you do not want to keep it.
evidence: Export the register as PDF or a screenshot.
A three-sentence summary for the fictional board: top risk, recommended treatment, decision needed.

labs.title: Classify and mark a test file share
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a new folder of dummy files you create yourself. Do not use real company documents or shares.
labs.goal: Practise applying a classification scheme by impact, marking files so the label travels with them, and spotting over-classification.
prerequisites: A computer with a word processor and a spreadsheet app
Cards: who classifies, marking vs labelling
Lesson 2.1 and 2.2
steps: Create a folder called LAB-share and 12 dummy files: for example a canteen menu, a press release, a staff phone list, a salary sheet, a board paper, a customer export, a draft contract, a published annual report, a password list (fake), a supplier price list, a patient list (fake names) and a project plan.
Write a four-level scheme with one line each: Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted, defined by the harm if disclosed.
For each file, write who the data owner would be in a real company and choose its level, with one sentence of reasoning.
Add a visible marking (header and footer) to every Confidential and Restricted file.
Add the level to each file's properties or metadata (for example the Tags or Keywords field).
Review your choices: move anything you rated higher than its real harm down a level, and note why.
Write one handling rule per level for storage, sending and destruction.
validation: Every file has an owner role and a level with a reason.
No more than a third of the files are at the top level; if more, you are over-classifying.
Confidential and Restricted files show the marking when printed or opened on another device.
Each level has storage, sending and destruction rules.
rollback: Delete the LAB-share folder. Nothing else is changed.
evidence: A table of file, owner role, level and reason.
A screenshot of one marked file and its metadata.
The one-page handling rules.

labs.title: See data remanence, then defeat it
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a spare USB stick or a virtual disk in a test VM that holds nothing you need. Never run recovery or wiping tools on a work device or a drive with real data.
labs.goal: Show that deleting and quick-formatting leave data recoverable, then sanitise the test media and show recovery fails.
prerequisites: A spare USB stick (8 GB or less is quickest) or a test VM with a second virtual disk
PhotoRec, the free open-source recovery tool from CGSecurity, downloaded from its official site
Card: clear, purge, destroy; drill: clear, purge, destroy
steps: Copy ten dummy files to the test media: a few photos you took yourself and some text files with a unique word such as LABMARKER in them.
Delete the files, empty the recycle bin and quick-format the media.
Run PhotoRec against the test media only, saving recovered files to a separate folder on your computer.
Count how many of the ten files came back, and search the recovered text files for LABMARKER.
Wipe the test media with a full overwrite (for example the operating system's full format, or a disk utility's zero-fill option).
Run PhotoRec again on the wiped media and count the recovered files.
Write two sentences on why this overwrite would not be enough for an SSD that held sensitive data.
validation: After the quick format, at least some files were recovered.
After the full overwrite, no LABMARKER files were recovered from the test media.
Your note mentions wear levelling or spare blocks, and names purge methods for SSDs (sanitise command or cryptographic erase).
rollback: Delete the recovered-files folder from your computer.
Reformat the test media for normal use, or delete the test VM's extra disk.
evidence: Screenshots of the PhotoRec results before and after the wipe.
Your counts and the two-sentence SSD note.

labs.title: Hashes vs signatures: tamper with a file and watch them fail
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a lab folder with dummy files you create. Do not sign real documents with lab keys.
labs.goal: Show that a hash detects change but proves nothing about who made the file, while a signature shows both integrity and origin.
prerequisites: OpenSSL 3.x
Drill: symmetric vs asymmetric vs hashing
An empty folder called LAB-sign
steps: Create a dummy file: `echo "Pay supplier 100" > order.txt`
Hash it: `openssl dgst -sha256 order.txt` and keep the digest.
Create a signing key pair: `openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out sign.key`, then `openssl pkey -in sign.key -pubout -out sign.pub`
Sign the file: `openssl pkeyutl -sign -inkey sign.key -rawin -in order.txt -out order.sig`
Verify it: `openssl pkeyutl -verify -pubin -inkey sign.pub -rawin -in order.txt -sigfile order.sig` (expect success).
Change 100 to 900 in order.txt, then repeat the hash and the verify; note what changed.
Write down why an attacker who changes the file can also publish a new matching hash, but cannot produce a valid signature without sign.key.
validation: The hash changes after editing the file.
Signature verification succeeds before the edit and fails after it.
Your note explains that a hash alone gives integrity but not origin.
rollback: Delete the LAB-sign folder, including sign.key.
evidence: The two digests and the two verify results.
Your one-paragraph explanation.

labs.title: Build a two-tier test PKI and inspect certificates
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a test VM or a lab folder on a personal machine, using names ending in .test. Never use these certificates or keys on real services, and never install the lab root in a production trust store.
labs.goal: See how a certificate chain is built and verified, and what changes when the wrong CA or an expired certificate is used.
prerequisites: OpenSSL 3.x (check with `openssl version`)
Lesson 3.6; card: TPM vs HSM
An empty folder called LAB-pki
steps: Create a lab root CA: `openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:3072 -nodes -keyout root.key -out root.crt -days 30 -subj "/CN=LAB Root CA"`
Create a key and request for a server: `openssl req -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout server.key -out server.csr -subj "/CN=portal.lab.test"`
Sign the request with the root: `openssl x509 -req -in server.csr -CA root.crt -CAkey root.key -CAcreateserial -out server.crt -days 7`
Verify the chain: `openssl verify -CAfile root.crt server.crt` (expect OK).
Inspect the certificate: `openssl x509 -in server.crt -noout -subject -issuer -dates` and note who issued it and when it expires.
Create a second, unrelated root (repeat step 1 with root2.key, root2.crt and CN=Other Root) and verify server.crt against root2.crt; note the error.
Write two sentences: what the root key's compromise would mean for every certificate it signed, and why real root keys live in HSMs.
validation: Verification succeeds against the lab root and fails against the unrelated root.
You can name the subject, issuer and validity dates of server.crt.
Your note mentions revoking and replacing everything the compromised root signed.
rollback: Delete the LAB-pki folder, including every .key file.
Nothing was installed into any trust store.
evidence: The output of both verify commands.
The subject, issuer and dates of server.crt.
Your two-sentence note.

labs.title: Scan a test VM and close what should not be open
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: scan only a virtual machine you own on an isolated or host-only network. Scanning systems you do not own or manage without written permission may be illegal.
labs.goal: Practise finding exposed services and reducing them with a host firewall, then prove the change.
prerequisites: A test VM (for example a Linux server) on a host-only network, and its IP address
Nmap installed from its official site on the host machine
Card: firewall types
steps: On the test VM, list listening services (on Linux: `ss -tulpn`).
From the host, scan the VM's common ports: `nmap -sT <vm-ip>` and note every open port.
Decide which services the VM needs; for a web test server that might be SSH and HTTP only.
Enable a host firewall on the VM that allows only those ports (on Ubuntu: `sudo ufw default deny incoming`, `sudo ufw allow 22/tcp`, `sudo ufw allow 80/tcp`, `sudo ufw enable`).
Scan again with the same command and compare the results.
Stop and disable one service the VM does not need, and confirm it no longer listens.
Write two sentences on why reducing listening services beats relying on the firewall alone.
validation: The second scan shows only the ports you chose as open.
The unneeded service no longer appears in the listening list.
Your note mentions defence in depth: the firewall and the service reduction each cover the other's failure.
rollback: On the VM, run `sudo ufw disable` and re-enable any service you stopped, or revert the VM to a snapshot.
evidence: Both scan outputs and the listening-services list before and after.
Your two-sentence note.

labs.title: See cleartext vs encrypted traffic with Wireshark
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: capture only your own traffic on your own machine or a test VM. Never capture on a work network or other people's traffic without written authorisation.
labs.goal: See what a network observer can read in cleartext protocols and what TLS hides, and connect it to OSI layers.
prerequisites: Wireshark installed from its official site
A browser on the same machine
Drill: which OSI layer?
steps: Start a capture on your active interface with the display filter `dns`.
Visit an ordinary website and find the DNS query for its name; note that the name is readable.
Change the filter to `tls.handshake.type == 1` and find the Client Hello for the same site; read the server name (SNI) field.
Change the filter to `http` and visit `http://neverssl.com`; open a packet and read the request in clear text.
Compare with an HTTPS page: follow the TLS stream and confirm the content is unreadable.
For one packet, expand each layer in the details pane and label it with its OSI layer (Ethernet, IP, TCP, TLS or HTTP).
Write three sentences on what an observer on hotel Wi-Fi could still learn about you even when every site uses HTTPS.
validation: You found a readable DNS name, a readable SNI and a readable HTTP request.
The HTTPS content is unreadable in the capture.
Your note mentions DNS names, SNI and traffic timing or volume as metadata that leaks.
rollback: Stop the capture and delete the capture file, which may contain your own browsing data.
evidence: Screenshots of the DNS query, the SNI field and the cleartext HTTP request.
Your three-sentence note.

labs.title: Run an access review in the test domain
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: the lab.test domain from day 9 only. Do not run discovery or review scripts against a real directory without authorisation.
labs.goal: Find privileged and dormant accounts with PowerShell, and practise the review decisions an owner would make.
prerequisites: The lab.test domain from day 9
Card: joiners, movers, leavers
steps: Create five extra test users, and leave two of them never signed in.
List privileged group members: `Get-ADGroupMember 'Domain Admins'` and `Get-ADGroupMember 'Enterprise Admins'`
Add one test user to Domain Admins 'temporarily', as many real environments do, then run the listing again.

Find accounts that have never been used or are inactive: `Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 -UsersOnly`, and `Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate | Select-Object Name, LastLogonDate`
Find accounts whose passwords never expire: `Search-ADAccount -PasswordNeverExpires -UsersOnly`
For each finding, record a decision as the owner would: keep, remove, disable, or investigate, with a one-line reason.
Apply your decisions: remove the extra Domain Admin and disable the unused accounts with `Disable-ADAccount`.
validation: Domain Admins contains only the built-in Administrator after clean-up.
Unused test accounts are disabled, not deleted, pending a decision.
Every finding has a recorded decision and reason.
rollback: Re-enable any account with `Enable-ADAccount`, or revert the VM snapshot.
evidence: The command outputs before and after clean-up.
Your decision table.

labs.title: Role-based access with groups in a test Active Directory
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a standalone Windows Server evaluation VM on an isolated network, with a domain named lab.test. Never run these commands on a production domain controller or a machine joined to a work domain.
labs.goal: Build role-based access with groups, see least privilege at work, and practise the joiner and mover steps.
prerequisites: A Windows Server evaluation VM with no network route to your work environment
An elevated PowerShell window on that VM
Drill: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC, rule-based
steps: Install the role: `Install-WindowsFeature AD-Domain-Services -IncludeManagementTools`
Create a test forest (the VM restarts): `Install-ADDSForest -DomainName lab.test -InstallDns`
Create an OU and two role groups: `New-ADOrganizationalUnit -Name LabUsers`, then `New-ADGroup -Name Role-Claims -GroupScope Global` and `New-ADGroup -Name Role-Finance -GroupScope Global`
Create two users with `New-ADUser` in the LabUsers OU (for example amai and tendai), and add amai to Role-Claims and tendai to Role-Finance with `Add-ADGroupMember`.
Create C:\LabShares\Claims and C:\LabShares\Finance, share them, and grant each role group Modify on its own folder only.
Sign in as each user (or use `runas`) and confirm each can open only their own folder.
Simulate a mover: move amai from Role-Claims to Role-Finance, then confirm she lost Claims access and gained Finance access after signing in again.
validation: Each user reaches only the folder for their role group.
After the move, amai has no access to Claims.
No permission was granted to an individual user; every grant goes to a group.
rollback: Delete the VM or revert it to the snapshot taken before the lab.
evidence: Screenshots of the two groups' members and the folder permissions.
A note of what changed for amai when she moved roles.

labs.title: Write rules of engagement for your test lab
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a paper exercise about your own lab VMs only. Do not use it to authorise testing of any system you do not own.
labs.goal: Practise the scoping and authorisation that make a test lawful and safe, using the lab from days 8 to 10.
prerequisites: The test VMs from earlier labs (or a list of imaginary ones)
Lesson 6.1; card: internal, external, third-party
steps: List the in-scope targets by name and IP address, and write an explicit out-of-scope list (for example your home router and work laptop).
Write the test window: dates and hours.
Name the authoriser (you, as owner of the lab), the tester, and an emergency contact.
Define stop conditions: for example, stop if a system becomes unstable or real personal data is found.
List permitted techniques (scanning, password guessing against lab accounts) and forbidden ones (denial of service, social engineering of real people).
Define how critical findings are reported during the test and how results are stored and destroyed afterwards.
Sign and date it as the authoriser.
validation: Every target is named, and out-of-scope items are explicit.
Stop conditions and an emergency contact are present.
The document is signed by someone with authority over every target (here, you).
rollback: Nothing to roll back: this is a document.
evidence: The signed one-page rules of engagement.

labs.title: Triage a vulnerability report by risk
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a paper exercise with fictional findings. Do not paste real scan results into public tools.
labs.goal: Practise prioritising remediation by exploitation evidence and asset criticality as well as severity.
prerequisites: A spreadsheet
Card: prioritising vulnerabilities
steps: Create ten fictional findings with columns: ID, system, internet-facing (yes/no), data handled, CVSS score, known exploited (yes/no).
Include at least: a critical flaw on an isolated test server, a medium flaw that is known exploited on an internet-facing payment server, and a high flaw on an internal HR system.
Give each system a tier: 1 (internet-facing with sensitive data), 2 (internal sensitive), 3 (other).
Write a priority rule, for example: known exploited plus tier 1 = fix in 48 hours; CVSS 9+ on tier 1 or 2 = 7 days; everything else by severity within 30 to 90 days.
Apply the rule and sort the list into a fix order.
Compare your order with a pure CVSS sort and note the three biggest differences.
Write the one-paragraph summary you would send to the CIO.
validation: The known-exploited flaw on the payment server is first.
The critical flaw on the isolated test server is not first.
The summary states business risk and dates, not just scores.
rollback: Nothing to roll back: fictional data only.
evidence: Your sorted list and priority rule.
The comparison with a pure CVSS sort and your CIO summary.

labs.title: Review Windows security event logs in the test domain
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: the lab.test domain from days 9 and 10 only. Do not export or examine logs from real systems without authorisation.
labs.goal: Generate and find the security events an analyst relies on: logons, failures, lockouts and privileged group changes.
prerequisites: The lab.test domain controller VM from day 9
An elevated PowerShell window on it
Cards: SIEM vs SOAR vs UEBA; chain of custody
steps: Set a lockout policy in the lab: open Group Policy Management, edit the Default Domain Policy, and set the account lockout threshold to 5 attempts.
Sign in as a test user with the wrong password six times, then sign in correctly as another test user.
Add a test user to Domain Admins, then remove them.
Find failed logons: `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 20 | Format-List TimeCreated, Message`
Find the lockout (event 4740) and the successful logon (4624), noting the logon type.
Find the privileged group change: `Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4728,4729} -MaxEvents 10`
Write a short incident note: what happened, when, which account, and what you would check next in a real investigation.
validation: You found events 4625, 4740, 4624 and 4728/4729 that match what you did.
Your note gives exact times and account names from the events.
Your note says what you would check next, such as the source workstation of the failures.
rollback: Reset the lockout threshold, unlock the test account with `Unlock-ADAccount`, or revert the VM snapshot.
evidence: Screenshots or exported text of each event you found.
Your incident note.

labs.title: Back up a test file share and prove you can restore it
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: the lab.test server VM with a second virtual disk for backups. Never practise restores over real data or on production servers.
labs.goal: Show that a backup is only proven by a restore, and measure how long recovery takes against an RTO you set.
prerequisites: The lab VM from day 9 with the C:\LabShares folders
A second virtual disk attached and formatted as E:
The Windows Server Backup feature: `Install-WindowsFeature Windows-Server-Backup`
steps: Set a target before you start: for example RTO 15 minutes, RPO the time of today's backup.
Back up the shares: `wbadmin start backup -backupTarget:E: -include:C:\LabShares -quiet`
Record the backup time, then add a new file to C:\LabShares\Claims after the backup.
Simulate a loss: delete the C:\LabShares\Claims folder.
List backup versions: `wbadmin get versions`, and note the version identifier.
Start a timer and restore: `wbadmin start recovery -version:<identifier> -itemType:File -items:C:\LabShares\Claims -recursive -recoveryTarget:C:\LabShares\Claims`
Check the restored files open, note which file was lost (the one added after the backup), and stop the timer.
validation: The folder is restored and its files open.
The file created after the backup is missing, showing what the RPO means in practice.
Your measured recovery time is recorded and compared with the RTO you set.
rollback: Delete the restored test data, or revert the VM snapshot.
evidence: The wbadmin output for backup, versions and recovery.
Your measured recovery time against the RTO, and a note on the lost file.

labs.title: Exploit and explain SQL injection in a local test app
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: OWASP Juice Shop, a deliberately vulnerable app, running in Docker on your own machine and bound to localhost only. Never test these techniques against any site you do not own.
labs.goal: See SQL injection work against a deliberately vulnerable app, then write down the structural fix.
prerequisites: Docker Desktop or Docker Engine on a personal machine
Drill: which fix stops this attack?
Card: attack and fix pairs
steps: Start Juice Shop on localhost only: `docker run --rm -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop`
Open `http://localhost:3000` in your browser and go to the login page.
Enter `' OR 1=1--` as the email and any password; note which account you are logged in as.
Explain in two sentences why that input changed the query's logic.
Write the vulnerable pattern (string concatenation) and the fixed pattern (a parameterised query) in pseudo-code side by side.
Try one more Juice Shop challenge from its scoreboard, such as a reflected XSS, and name its structural fix.
Stop the container with Ctrl+C.
validation: You logged in without a valid password using injection.
Your fixed pseudo-code passes the email as a parameter, not as part of the SQL string.
You named output encoding as the fix for the XSS challenge.
rollback: Stop the container; the --rm flag removes it. Optionally remove the image with `docker rmi bkimminich/juice-shop`.
evidence: A screenshot of the logged-in session.
Your vulnerable and fixed pseudo-code and explanations.

labs.title: Generate an SBOM and audit dependencies
labs.environment: LAB / TEST ENVIRONMENT: a throwaway Node.js project in a lab folder. Do not run these tools against company repositories without approval.
labs.goal: See how an SBOM lists components and how dependency auditing finds known vulnerabilities, including old versions you pinned on purpose.
prerequisites: Node.js and npm installed
An empty folder called LAB-sbom
Card: open-source risk; card: software bill of materials
steps: Create a project: `npm init -y`
Install an old library version on purpose: `npm install lodash@4.17.15`
Audit dependencies: `npm audit` and note the severity and advisory for lodash.
Generate a CycloneDX SBOM: `npx @cyclonedx/cyclonedx-npm --output-file sbom.json`
Open sbom.json and find the lodash entry, its version and its package URL.
Upgrade: `npm install lodash@latest`, then run `npm audit` again and compare.
Write two sentences on how an SBOM would help if a new lodash flaw were announced tomorrow.
validation: The first audit reports at least one lodash advisory; the second does not.
sbom.json lists lodash with its version.
Your note explains finding affected products quickly from the SBOM.
evidence: Both npm audit outputs.
The lodash entry from sbom.json and your note.
